title: Urban Planning
description: Ten calm, informative texts on how cities are shaped: Jane Jacobs and the sidewalk, Central Park, the grid and the winding street, empty plazas, the High Line, zoning, a planner's life, the fifteen-minute city, cities built on water and the plan of Washington.

lessons.title: The Ballet of Hudson Street
lessons.summary: Jane Jacobs watches her own block in Greenwich Village and explains why lively sidewalks keep a city safe.
lessons.text:
In 1961, Jane Jacobs published a book that changed the way many people look at cities. It was called The Death and Life of Great American Cities, and it opened with a bold claim: the planners of her time, with their towers and highways, did not understand how cities work. She was not a planner but a journalist who lived above a candy store on Hudson Street in Greenwich Village, and she had learned about cities by watching her own block.

What she saw, she described as a kind of ballet. Each morning the sidewalk filled in a familiar order. Shop owners rolled up their metal gates. Children walked to school. Dog owners appeared, each holding a leash, and at the end of each leash was a dog with firm opinions about every corner. Later came shoppers carrying tote bags and the steady chatter of people meeting at the corner. In the barber shop, men argued about the latest hairstyles; at the grocery, the chatter was about prices, the weather and, now and then, somebody's surprising new hairstyle. No playwright had written this performance, yet it had its own order and timing, and a playwright could hardly have invented a better cast.

From this ordinary scene she inferred something important. A street is safe, she argued, not mainly because of the police but because of what she called "eyes on the street": shop owners, residents at their windows, people passing with their tote bags. A burglary is harder to commit when someone is always watching. From the constant presence of ordinary people, Jacobs inferred that a lively street largely protects itself. Where the sidewalk empties at night, burglary and street crime find room.

Jacobs cared intensely about details that planners ignored: short blocks, which give walkers many routes; old buildings mixed with new ones, so that small businesses can afford the rent; and enough residents to keep the shops busy. She felt intensely that these details were connected. Remove one, she warned, and the whole fabric of a neighborhood could begin to unravel, like a sweater when a single thread is pulled.

She did more than write. When the powerful official Robert Moses planned to extend a road through Washington Square Park, Jacobs joined the residents who fought the plan, and the park was eventually closed to cars. Later she helped defeat a planned highway across lower Manhattan, which, she believed, would have made the life of the old streets unravel.

Critics point out that the streets she loved have become very expensive, yet her central lesson remains: to understand a city, walk its sidewalks and watch.

Questions:
Where did Jane Jacobs learn about cities?
She learned about cities by watching her own block on Hudson Street in Greenwich Village.
Who appeared on the sidewalk in the morning?
Shop owners, children, dog owners holding a leash, and shoppers with tote bags appeared.
What did Jacobs infer from the constant presence of ordinary people?
She inferred that a lively street largely protects itself.
Why did she care so intensely about small details?
She believed they were connected, so that if one was removed, the whole neighborhood could begin to unravel.
What did she do about the road through Washington Square Park?
She joined the residents who fought the plan, and the park was eventually closed to cars.

lessons.title: A Park Made to Look Untouched
lessons.summary: Olmsted and Vaux turn rough, rocky land into Central Park, a designed landscape that looks natural.
lessons.text:
Visitors to Central Park often assume that its rocks, meadows, winding paths and quiet water have been there forever. In fact, almost every view was made by hand. Its natural look is its most careful illusion.

In 1857, New York held a competition to design a large public park. The winning plan came from two men: Frederick Law Olmsted, a former farmer and journalist with no training as a designer, and Calvert Vaux, an architect born in London.

The land they were given was far from beautiful. It was rocky and wet, crossed by streams, and dotted with small farms and shacks where poor families kept pigs and goats. It also held Seneca Village, a settled community of mostly Black property owners, with homes, churches and a school. The city took the land, and about 1,600 people, from the shacks and from Seneca Village alike, had to leave. Their story is now rightly told as part of the park's history.

Workers blasted rock, moved earth and dug lakes where there had been swamps. Millions of trees and shrubs were planted. Many of them were propagated in nurseries, where gardeners grew young plants from seeds and cuttings until they were strong enough to be moved. Trees that could not be propagated quickly enough were brought in already grown.

The designers solved one problem with special skill. The city needed roads across the park, and carts would have broken its calm. So Olmsted and Vaux sank these roads below the level of the park, hidden by walls and planting. Separate paths serve carriages, riders and walkers, with bridges where they cross. It is a finely tuned system, and the views are just as finely balanced, opening and closing as a walker moves.

Olmsted believed the park had a moral purpose. He hoped that rich and poor would share the same lawns, and that green space would make city life more civilized: calmer and kinder. A civilized city, he felt, needed a place to rest the eyes. He also cared about what we now call wellbeing: scenery, he wrote, could restore tired minds, and modern research on the wellbeing of city residents tends to support him.

He even planted thick borders of trees to hide the surrounding city. He could not have imagined the skyline that rises there today. Now the towers of the skyline stand above those trees, and many visitors love the contrast. When the first snow falls, children slide down the hills in pure ecstasy, and their parents remember the same ecstasy from long ago.

Central Park helped redefine what a city park could be. Before it, people in many cities strolled in cemeteries for lack of anywhere better; after it, dozens of cities wanted a great park of their own. Olmsted himself went on to redefine landscapes from Brooklyn to Chicago.

Questions:
What did the land look like before the park was built?
It was rocky and wet, with small farms and shacks.
What happened to the people of Seneca Village?
The city took the land, and they had to leave.
How were many of the plants propagated?
They were propagated in nurseries from seeds and cuttings.
Why did Olmsted and Vaux sink the roads across the park?
They sank them so that traffic would not break the calm of the park.
How did Olmsted think the park would affect city life?
He hoped it would make city life more civilized and support wellbeing.

lessons.title: The Grid and the Winding Street
lessons.summary: Manhattan's grid, Broadway's diagonal, crooked old towns and modern dead ends are compared.
lessons.text:
A map of Manhattan north of 14th Street shows a grid: long avenues running north and south, crossed at right angles by numbered streets. It was laid down by a plan of 1811, when most of the island was still farms and woods. Its authors explained their reasoning simply: houses with straight sides and right angles, they wrote, are the cheapest to build and the most convenient to live in. The grid divided the land systematically into lots that could be bought, sold and built on, block after block.

One old road refused to obey. Broadway, older than the plan, runs at an angle and punctures the grid. Wherever it crosses an avenue, it leaves an odd open space, and those punctures became famous squares: Madison Square, Herald Square, Times Square.

The winding street has a longer history. Many old towns in Europe grew without a single plan; their streets followed hills, rivers, old paths and walls. In Boston, a popular legend says that the crooked streets of the old center follow the paths of cows. Historians find the story doubtful, but the streets really do seem to wander.

Grids are ancient too. Roman army camps were laid out in straight lines, and the Spanish built new towns systematically around a central plaza with straight streets. On a flat mesa or a broad plain, a grid fits the land easily. On steep hills it does not. In San Francisco, the grid was drawn over the hills as if they were a flat mesa, and some streets climb so sharply that stairs replace the sidewalk.

Which pattern is better? Defenders of the grid underline its clarity. A stranger can find an address, and traffic has many routes. Defenders of the winding street underline its charm: views open and close, and drivers slow down.

The modern suburb offers a third pattern. Many suburbs built in the last century used loops and dead ends. The streets are quiet, but they are often disconnected from one another. A house may stand a few hundred yards from a store and still be a two-mile drive away, because the streets between them are disconnected.

Planners now try to measure such differences. One common method counts intersections per square mile. The count is only an estimation of how easy an area is to walk, but by this estimation old grids and old winding towns both do well, while many suburbs do poorly.

So is the grid overrated? Perhaps the question itself is overrated. It is doubtful that any single shape is best everywhere. What seems to matter most is whether streets connect.

Questions:
Why did the authors of the 1811 plan prefer straight lines and right angles?
They wrote that such houses are the cheapest to build and the most convenient to live in.
What does Broadway do to the grid?
It runs at an angle and punctures the grid, leaving open spaces that became famous squares.
Why do many historians find the Boston legend doubtful?
They doubt that the crooked streets really follow the paths of cows.
What happened when the grid was drawn over the hills of San Francisco?
Some streets climb so sharply that stairs replace the sidewalk.
Why can a store near a suburban house be a long drive away?
The streets between them are disconnected.

lessons.title: Why Some Plazas Stay Empty
lessons.summary: William H. Whyte films the plazas of New York and finds out what makes people stay.
lessons.text:
In 1961, New York offered developers a bargain: build a public plaza at the foot of your office tower, and you may build extra floors above it. Dozens of plazas appeared across Manhattan. Many of them were nearly empty.

The writer William Whyte wanted to know why. In 1970 he began what he called the Street Life Project, and he studied plazas the way a scientist studies birds. His team filmed the same spaces from nearby roofs, day after day. The aperture of each lens, the opening that lets in the light, had to be set for bright noon and cloudy afternoons alike, and a wrong aperture could ruin a day of film. Whyte wanted to quantify what most people only feel: who came, where they sat, how long they stayed. Once the behavior was quantified, the patterns were plain to see.

The key finding was almost too simple: people sit where there are places to sit. Many plazas offered handsome stone and little else. Their ledges were too high or too narrow, and some were even fitted with metal spikes to repel anyone who might want to rest. Such details repel people as surely as a locked gate. The omission of seating was not an accident of style but a decision, and its result was empty space. The omission of sun, trees and food had much the same effect.

Comfort mattered in small ways. A bench of rough wood that splinters after a few winters will soon be avoided, since nobody wants a splinter with lunch. Chairs that could be moved worked wonders: people would shift one a few inches before sitting, as if the gesture gave them control.

Above all, people like to watch other people, and a busy plaza is a stage. Office workers stroll past in their best clothes, and some walk as proudly as a peacock. The peacock needs an audience, and the people on the benches gladly provide it.

Wind can spoil everything. A tall tower may push fast air down to the street, and at its corners the air can spin into a small vortex that lifts dust and paper. A plaza caught in such a vortex will stay empty. In many plazas today, the only crowd is a group of smokers by the door, held there by nicotine rather than by design, and nicotine is a poor substitute for a pleasant place.

Whyte admired Paley Park, a tiny space on East 53rd Street with light chairs, trees and a waterfall across its back wall. The rush of the water covers the growl of traffic. A visitor a few steps from the street almost forgets the growl of the city.

In 1975, partly because of Whyte's research, the city rewrote its rules, and new plazas had to offer seating, trees and other comforts.

Questions:
Why did developers build so many plazas after 1961?
The new rules let them build extra floors if they built a public plaza.
Why did Whyte's team have to set the aperture of each lens carefully?
A wrong aperture could ruin a day of film.
What was Whyte's key finding?
He found that people sit where there are places to sit.
What can a vortex do to a plaza?
A vortex of wind can lift dust and paper, so the plaza stays empty.
How does the waterfall in Paley Park help visitors?
The rush of the water covers the growl of traffic.

lessons.title: The Railway in the Sky
lessons.summary: An abandoned elevated railway on Manhattan's West Side is saved by two residents and becomes the High Line.
lessons.text:
In the early twentieth century, freight trains ran at street level on the West Side of Manhattan, and they killed so many people that Tenth Avenue was nicknamed "Death Avenue." The solution, opened in 1934, was an elevated railway that lifted the trains above the streets and even ran through some buildings.

Its first incarnation did not last long. Trucks took over most of the work, and the last train ran in 1980. Seeds carried by wind and birds took root in the gravel, and grasses, wild flowers and small trees spread along the tracks. In spring, caterpillars crawled along the stems, and butterflies followed. Seen from the street, the long green line resting between buildings looked a little like a giant caterpillar itself.

Many owners of the land below wanted it removed, arguing that it was ugly and that any delay would endanger the future of the neighborhood. Around the turn of the century, a plan to tear it down seemed close, endangering what was left of the old line.

In 1999, two residents, Joshua David and Robert Hammond, met at a community meeting and decided to save it. Neither was an expert in planning. Some people called them fanatics, and the idea seemed to many the dream of a fanatic. What they had was persistence. For years they held meetings, raised money and showed photographs of the wild gardens. Their persistence slowly changed minds, and in 2002 the city began to support the project.

A design competition followed. When the winning team showed its first renditions of the new park, people could see a path curving through the old plants, with benches that seemed to grow out of the concrete. Each rendition kept the old rails visible here and there. The Dutch garden designer Piet Oudolf chose grasses and flowers that echo the wild plants that had grown there on their own. In late summer the result looks less like a formal garden than a loose, enormous bouquet, a bouquet that changes every week.

The first section of the High Line's new incarnation opened in 2009. It was a sensational success, and millions of people now visit every year. Not all of its effects were so sensational in a happy sense. The rules for the surrounding area had been changed, and for owners of nearby land the park was a jackpot: property values rose sharply, and new towers appeared along its length. Many long-time residents did not share in the jackpot; they faced rising rents instead. Hammond later said publicly that the project should have done more for the communities around it.

The High Line teaches two lessons: an old structure can be given a second life, and that life will change the streets below it.

Questions:
Why was the elevated railway built?
It was built to lift the freight trains above the streets.
What grew on the tracks after the trains stopped?
Grasses, wild flowers and small trees grew there, and caterpillars crawled along the stems.
What did Joshua David and Robert Hammond have, according to the text?
They had persistence, and it slowly changed minds.
What did the first renditions of the new park show?
They showed a path curving through the old plants, with the rails visible here and there.
Why was the park a jackpot for owners of nearby land?
Property values rose sharply, and new towers appeared along its length.

lessons.title: Zoning, Explained
lessons.summary: A short guide to what zoning is, where it came from and why it is argued about.
lessons.text:
Zoning is the set of local rules that decides what may be built where. A zoning map divides a town into districts, each with its own rules: whether buildings may hold homes, shops or factories, and how tall they may be.

The idea grew out of an old branch of law. For centuries, courts had dealt with the nuisance: a factory whose smoke dirtied the laundry of the houses around it, a yard full of noisy animals. A resident could go to court over a nuisance, but only after the harm had been done. Zoning was an attempt to prevent such harm in advance.

In 1915, the huge Equitable Building rose in lower Manhattan and cast a long shadow over the streets around it. The next year, New York adopted the first zoning law for an entire city in the United States. It required tall buildings to step back from the street as they rose, so that light could reach the sidewalk. That rule explains why many older towers in New York look like wedding cakes. In 1926, the Supreme Court approved zoning in a case from the village of Euclid, Ohio. In a famous image, the judge who wrote the decision compared a nuisance to a pig in the living room: acceptable in one place and wrong in another.

Zoning must work with the existent city, not an imagined one. Most codes allow existent buildings to remain if they broke no rule when they were built, even if they would not be allowed today. When an owner wants an exception, a procedural path begins: public notice, a hearing, and a vote by a board. These procedural steps protect fairness but can take months. When residents and builders cannot agree, some cities offer mediation, in which a neutral person helps both sides seek a compromise. Mediation is often quicker than a lawsuit.

Zoning touches personal finances too. When a bank lends money for a house, it orders an appraisal of the property. Because zoning decides what can be built on a lot, it can change an appraisal a great deal. Residents often fear that a new building will put the value of their home in jeopardy; a builder may feel that a long delay puts the whole project in jeopardy.

In recent years, the cost of housing has pushed zoning to the forefront of public debate. Some economists argue that rules allowing only one house per lot limit the supply of homes and raise prices. Others answer that such rules protect quiet streets. Both concerns are at the forefront of planning today.

Architects have their own complaint: that rigid rules produce mediocre buildings, designed to fit the rules rather than the street. Planners reply that a mediocre building in the right place does less harm than a brilliant one in the wrong place.

Questions:
What does a zoning map do?
It divides a town into districts, and each district has its own rules.
How was zoning different from the old law of nuisance?
Courts dealt with a nuisance after the harm was done; zoning tried to prevent it.
Why do many older towers in New York look like wedding cakes?
A rule required tall buildings to step back from the street as they rose.
What happens in mediation?
A neutral person helps both sides seek a compromise.
Why can zoning change an appraisal?
Zoning decides what can be built on a lot, so it affects the value of the property.

lessons.title: A Planner's Life
lessons.summary: A profile of Marta Delgado, who spent almost forty years planning streets in a river city.
lessons.text:
When Marta Delgado joined the planning department of her river city in 1986, she was the only woman among twelve planners. Sexism was simply part of the furniture. At meetings, men asked her to take notes. Developers directed their questions to her younger male assistant. She did not argue; she prepared more carefully than anyone else. "Sexism is tiring," she said, "but it is not as strong as a well-prepared woman with the right numbers."

Her advantage was language. Delgado grew up with grandparents who spoke only Spanish, and she is fluent in both Spanish and English. On the east side of the city, many families spoke Spanish at home, and few came to meetings held only in English. She began to hold every meeting there in both languages. Residents fluent only in Spanish began to attend.

From the start, she recorded meetings on a small cassette recorder, and she still keeps hundreds of cassettes in boxes in her office, each labeled with a street and a date. When a dispute arose years later, she could find the right cassette and play back exactly what had been promised.

At home, she likes to tinker. On weekends her kitchen table is covered with cardboard models of bus shelters and benches. She will tinker with a single model for hours, moving a bench a fraction of an inch until a shelter feels open rather than enclosed.

Her favorite tool is her own hand. On the paper maps she used for decades, the width of her pinky was roughly a five-minute walk. At public meetings she would lay her pinky on the map, again and again, and ask a simple question: "Can a child walk from here to the school?"

Her greatest project was the path along the river, a strip of trees, lights and benches that took eleven years to finish. The last two years brought many evening hearings, and the long nights gave her migraines. On the worst evenings she kept a migraine pill beside her glass of water.

Outside work, she plays the harp. Her daughter plays the flute, and for several summers the two of them have performed a duet at the concerts held beside the river path. A harp and a flute are both quiet instruments, and the duet works only if each player listens closely to the other. Delgado says that planning is much the same.

She retires this year. Her pension will be paid as an annuity, a fixed sum every month for the rest of her life. She laughs that the annuity will cover harp strings and travel. She also plans to keep attending meetings, this time as a resident.

Questions:
What was Delgado's experience of sexism when she started?
Men asked her to take notes, and developers directed their questions to her younger male assistant.
Why did she hold meetings in two languages?
Many families on the east side spoke Spanish at home, and she is fluent in both languages.
Why are her cassettes useful?
She could play back exactly what had been promised.
How did she use her pinky at meetings?
She laid it on the map, because its width was roughly a five-minute walk.
What does Delgado say a duet and planning have in common?
Both work only if each person listens closely to the other.

lessons.title: The Fifteen-Minute City, Weighed Calmly
lessons.summary: A balanced look at the idea that daily needs should lie within a short walk or ride of home.
lessons.text:
In a fifteen-minute city, most of the things people need every day, such as groceries, schools, a doctor, a park and perhaps a job, lie within a fifteen-minute walk or bicycle ride of home. The phrase was made popular by Carlos Moreno, a researcher in Paris, and it became widely known in 2020, when the mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, made it part of her campaign. The idea itself is older: in 1929, the planner Clarence Perry described a neighborhood built around a school that every child could reach on foot.

Planners describe the goal with the word accessibility. The question is not how fast you can travel but how many useful places you can reach in a given time. Good accessibility also means that an older person, or someone in a wheelchair, can reach them easily.

Picture a parent who needs milk, bread and a bunch of kale for dinner. In one neighborhood, the kale is a five-minute walk away, past a library, a pharmacy and a flower shop with orchids in the window. In another, the same kale requires a car and a parking lot. The first parent may never notice the orchids, but the walk adds something to the day.

Would fifteen minutes suffice for everything? For groceries and school, often. For work, much less often: many jobs lie across town. Nor can a small local clinic suffice for serious illness. The honest version of the idea is a goal for daily life, not a promise about all of life.

What does the evidence say? Much of it is qualitative: interviews in which residents describe how they shop, whom they meet and how safe they feel. Qualitative studies suggest that people who walk to daily shops often know more people nearby, but they do not prove that the idea works everywhere.

Critics raise fair concerns. When a neighborhood becomes pleasant and convenient, prices tend to rise. Rising rents can act as a canary in the coal mine, an early warning that the people the plan was meant to help may be pushed out. Careful planners watch that canary closely. Others note that in the suburbs and the countryside, distances are too large for any such promise.

Incidentally, the debate has not always been calm. Online rumors claimed that the idea was a scheme to keep people inside their districts, and some of the messages sent to local planners were hateful. A hateful message, however, is not an argument. It would be dishonest to call the idea a plot; it measures distance, it does not lock any gates. It would be equally dishonest to promise that short distances alone will cure every problem of a city.

Incidentally, before cars nearly everyone lived in a fifteen-minute city, simply because walking was the only choice.

Questions:
What does a fifteen-minute city offer?
Most daily needs lie within a fifteen-minute walk or bicycle ride of home.
What do planners mean by accessibility?
They mean how many useful places you can reach in a given time.
Why would fifteen minutes not suffice for work?
Many jobs lie across town, too far for a short walk.
What kind of evidence is qualitative?
Interviews in which residents describe their daily lives are qualitative evidence.
Why can rising rents be a canary in the coal mine?
They are an early warning that the people the plan was meant to help may be pushed out.

lessons.title: Cities Built on Water
lessons.summary: Amsterdam, Leiden and Venice show how fish, floods and fresh water shaped the plans of cities.
lessons.text:
An old Dutch proverb says that Amsterdam was built on herring bones. Like most proverbs, it exaggerates, but it holds a truth. For centuries, herring from the North Sea, salted and packed in barrels, made Dutch ports rich. Fishermen brought the herring ashore by the ton. The money paid for warehouses, ships and, in time, one of the most famous pieces of planning in Europe: the ring of canals that Amsterdam began to dig in 1613, three main canals curving around the old center in wide half circles.

Another proverb says that God made the world, but the Dutch made the Netherlands. Much of the country lies below the level of the sea, held dry by dikes and pumps. Water was both a threat and a weapon. In 1574, the city of Leiden was surrounded by a Spanish army, and its people came close to starvation. The rebels broke the dikes and flooded the land, so that ships could sail over the fields to the city walls. They arrived on October 3 with herring and white bread, and Leiden was saved from starvation. Each year on that date, the people of Leiden still eat herring and white bread to remember.

Venice faced the opposite problem. The city stands on small islands in a shallow lagoon, and the lagoon protected it from armies for a thousand years. On a clear morning the water can look like a sheet of sapphire, and the domes seem to float on the sapphire surface. But the water around the city is salty, and freshwater was always scarce. The Venetians solved this with remarkable planning. Under many of their squares they built large tanks lined with clay and filled with sand. Rain ran into the sand, was cleaned as it sank, and collected in a central well. The stone well heads still stand in the squares today, though the city now receives freshwater through pipes.

The lagoon and the open sea also brought danger. Piracy was a constant threat to trade, and the Venetian navy spent centuries fighting piracy along the coasts. The tall bell tower beside the church of San Marco served as a sentinel, a watchtower and a lighthouse for ships approaching the city. Sailors coming ashore after a long voyage would look for that sentinel above the roofs.

Cities on water face one more danger, and it is quieter. When drinking water and waste are not kept apart, diseases spread: cholera, typhoid and hepatitis. Hepatitis A, in particular, still spreads wherever water is unsafe. Much of modern city planning, from sewers to treatment plants, is the patient business of keeping clean and dirty water apart.

Questions:
What does the old Dutch proverb say about Amsterdam?
It says that Amsterdam was built on herring bones.
How was Leiden saved from starvation in 1574?
The rebels broke the dikes and flooded the land, so ships could sail to the city walls with herring and bread.
Why was freshwater scarce in Venice?
The city stands in a lagoon, and the water around it is salty.
How did the Venetians collect clean water?
Rain ran into sand under the squares, was cleaned as it sank, and collected in a central well.
What did the bell tower of San Marco do for sailors?
It served as a sentinel and a lighthouse that sailors looked for when they came ashore.

lessons.title: A Capital Drawn on Paper
lessons.summary: How Washington was planned, burned, rebuilt and finally made to follow its original drawing.
lessons.text:
In June 1783, several hundred unpaid soldiers surrounded the building in Philadelphia where Congress was meeting. Under the Articles of Confederation, the national government was weak, and the state authorities did not send troops to protect it. Congress left the city for Princeton. Members spoke of anarchy, and the fear of anarchy stayed with them. When the Constitution replaced the Confederation a few years later, it allowed Congress to create a federal district under its own control, so that the government would never again depend on a single state for its safety. 

In 1790, Congress chose a site on the Potomac River. The next year, President Washington asked Pierre Charles L'Enfant, a French-born engineer who had served in the Revolution, to design the new city. The boundaries were surveyed by Andrew Ellicott with the help of Benjamin Banneker, a free Black mathematician and astronomer. Banneker spent long nights watching the sky, measuring the positions of the stars as each constellation crossed overhead, in order to fix the exact starting point of the survey. For him, every constellation was a precise instrument.

L'Enfant's plan was bold. Over a grid of streets he laid broad diagonal avenues that started from the Capitol and the President's House, with circles and squares where they met. Between the Capitol and the river he drew a long public garden, the ancestor of today's National Mall. L'Enfant was proud and difficult, and after many quarrels he was dismissed in 1792. Ellicott revised the plan, and it was engraved on copper and printed, so that buyers of land could see what the city would become.

In 1814, troops from Britain entered Washington and set fire to the Capitol and the President's House. They acted partly to avenge the burning of York, the capital of Upper Canada, by United States troops the year before. The fires caused great havoc, and only a heavy storm the next day kept the havoc from spreading further. York had been avenged, but the government stayed, and the buildings were rebuilt.

The young capital also saw new technology. In 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message by telegraph from the Capitol to Baltimore, using the system of short and long signals now called Morse code. Morse code would carry news around the world for a century.

By 1900, however, much of L'Enfant's vision had been lost. A railroad station and its tracks stood on the Mall. In 1902, a commission proposed a plan that sought fidelity to L'Enfant's original drawing: the tracks were removed, and the Mall became an open green space framed by museums. Its fidelity to the old plan was not perfect, but it was close. In 1909, L'Enfant's remains were moved to Arlington, where his plan of the city is engraved on the stone above his grave.

Questions:
Why did Congress leave Philadelphia in 1783?
Unpaid soldiers surrounded its building, and the state authorities did not send troops to protect it.
How did Banneker help the survey?
He measured the positions of the stars as each constellation crossed overhead to fix the starting point.
Why was the plan engraved and printed?
It was engraved so that buyers of land could see what the city would become.
Why did troops from Britain burn Washington, according to the text?
They acted partly to avenge the burning of York by United States troops.
What did the plan of 1902 seek?
It sought fidelity to L'Enfant's original drawing.
